idiom_name: unexported resource type with a checked method, wrapped by http.Handler middleware carrying the principal in context.Context
implementation_notes: Go has no access modifiers, but it has package privacy: an identifier that is not exported (first character not upper case, per the language specification) is reachable only from its own package, so a vault struct with unexported fields and a single exported method that consults the policy is the idiom that replaces the classic guard object - no other package can construct it or touch its fields. For request-driven code the always-invoked property comes from the handler chain: middleware decorates every route, and the request-scoped principal travels in context.Context, which the Go blog documents as the carrier for the identity of the end user and authorization tokens. Because http.Handler is an interface, the wrapper can be composed and the policy swapped without touching the resource; the classic struct-and-interface form is still justified when the resource is reached outside HTTP, and then the unexported type plus checked method is the whole mediator.
pitfalls: A missing principal in context.Context is silent: ctx.Value(key) returns nil, and a mediator that treats nil as unrestricted fails open - deny when the identity is absent.
Middleware is only as complete as its registration: handlers mounted on a bare mux, or registered before the wrapper is applied, never pass the mediator.
Goroutines started with context.Background() (or any fresh context) lose the principal, so the work they do runs with no identity and no check.
Exported fields or an exported constructor let callers build the resource directly and call its methods unmediated; keep the type unexported and hand out only the mediated interface.
